heuristics.rule: Counter at 10–20% above the initial offer in round one
heuristics.condition: When you receive an initial offer and are preparing your first counter
heuristics.action: Ask for 10–20% above the initial number as your opening counter
heuristics.because: Companies typically move 40–60% toward your ask in round one, so anchoring higher gives you room to land at your actual target

heuristics.rule: If base feels locked, shift to signing bonus or equity
heuristics.condition: When the company signals the base salary is at its ceiling but negotiation isn't fully resolved
heuristics.action: Move the conversation to signing bonus, equity, or other levers instead of continuing to push base
heuristics.because: Different budget pools exist for different comp components; what's frozen in one lever may be available in another

heuristics.rule: Stop at round three; never push to round four or five
heuristics.condition: When you've already completed two or three rounds of back-and-forth
heuristics.action: Treat round three as the closing round and make your final ask there
heuristics.because: Pushing to a fourth or fifth round signals you're maximizing extraction rather than finding mutual agreement, damaging the relationship before day one

heuristics.rule: 'Final offer' in an email still has room; 'final offer' on a phone call with a hard deadline does not
heuristics.condition: When the recruiter uses the phrase 'final offer'
heuristics.action: Assess the delivery channel and tone — if email, request a call; if phone with a deadline and matter-of-fact tone, treat it as genuinely final
heuristics.because: The phrase 'final offer' is often a negotiating position, not a hard limit, but context signals whether room remains

heuristics.rule: Use the closing script when you're within 5% of your target number
heuristics.condition: When total comp is close to your goal and you want to close without damaging goodwill
heuristics.action: Say: 'Thank you for going to bat for me on this. If we can get to [final number], I'm ready to sign today.'
heuristics.because: This creates urgency, preserves the relationship, and gives the company a clear path to resolution rather than leaving them uncertain

heuristics.rule: Share the competing offer number but not the company name
heuristics.condition: When you have a competing offer and want to use it as leverage
heuristics.action: Disclose the dollar amount without naming the competing employer
heuristics.because: The number is what creates leverage; naming the company invites verification and comparison that can derail the conversation

heuristics.rule: Calculate your BATNA before entering any negotiation conversation
heuristics.condition: Before you begin any salary negotiation
heuristics.action: Determine the specific number below which you will walk away, based on your current comp, financial needs, and non-cash factors
heuristics.because: Without a walk-away number you'll either accept something bad or overplay your hand; the BATNA is the anchor that keeps both mistakes in check

heuristics.rule: Request a deadline extension first, then use that time to generate a competing offer
heuristics.condition: When you have an offer but no competing offer yet and need more time
heuristics.action: Ask for an extension framed as needing time for a thoughtful decision, then actively interview during that window
heuristics.because: Extensions are almost always granted, and the time can be used to manufacture real leverage rather than artificial urgency

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Your walk-away alternative determines how much pressure you can credibly apply; weak BATNA means the company can hold firm and you have no exit
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Identify your actual best alternative — current job, competing offer, or nothing — and honestly evaluate whether you would act on it

decision_factors.why_it_matters: A real competing offer is the single strongest lever in negotiation; it creates urgency, imports a deadline, and forces the target company to act
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Do you have a written or verbal offer with a specific number from another employer that you would genuinely consider accepting?

decision_factors.factor: Where current total comp sits relative to levels.fyi median
decision_factors.why_it_matters: If the offer is already at or above market median, there is structurally less room to push; continuing signals you are extracting rather than calibrating to market
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Look up the role, level, and location on levels.fyi and compare the full offer package — base, equity, bonus — against the median

decision_factors.why_it_matters: The recruiter's affect is a real-time signal of whether room remains; a shift from collaborative to administrative signals you've reached the ceiling
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Notice whether the recruiter is still problem-solving with you or has become transactional and matter-of-fact in their language

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Once you've moved on base, equity, and signing bonus and the company has responded to all three, the negotiation space is exhausted
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Count how many compensation components you've negotiated; if all three major levers are resolved, treat the package as final

decision_factors.factor: Whether the candidate would actually leave for the BATNA
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Leverage that you would not actually use is not real leverage; the company may sense this and hold firm accordingly
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask yourself honestly: if this company doesn't move, will I actually take my alternative? If the answer is no, your stated leverage is weaker than it appears

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Post-acceptance negotiation only works if backed by demonstrated delivery; without it, the ask reads as entitlement rather than market correction
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Have you delivered measurably beyond the original job scope, received strong feedback, or seen your responsibilities expand since joining?

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Pushing to a fourth or fifth negotiation round
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: You enter day one with the perception of being a difficult or extractive employee, which can subtly affect your manager's advocacy for you in future reviews
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates who optimize for maximum extraction without understanding the relationship cost

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Manufacturing a fake competing offer to gain leverage
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Recruiters verify offers and if caught, the offer is typically rescinded and your professional reputation in that company's network is damaged
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates without real competing offers who feel pressured to fabricate one

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting an offer without knowing your BATNA
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: You lose the ability to walk away when you should, meaning you may accept a package below your actual floor because you have no pre-committed reference point
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: First-time negotiators and people who are emotionally attached to a specific offer or company

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Backing out of an accepted offer after receiving a competing offer
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: While there is no legal liability before a start date, there is a real reputational cost that can follow you, especially in tight-knit industries or if the recruiter moves to another company
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates in small industries or who may encounter the same recruiters again

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Using speed creation ('I'll sign today if you hit X') as a closing tactic
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: If the company calls your bluff and doesn't move, you've either signed at a number you settled for or you must back down, weakening your credibility in the negotiation
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates who use urgency tactics without being genuinely prepared to follow through

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Framing post-acceptance negotiation as a comp ask without performance data
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: It signals to your manager that you were strategically underbidding at hire, which can erode trust even if the ask is granted
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: New employees who attempt post-acceptance negotiation too early or without clear delivery evidence

failure_patterns.pattern: Stopping negotiation after the first company counter
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates experience relief when the company moves at all and interpret any upward movement as the ceiling, not understanding the typical three-round arc
failure_patterns.consequence: Leaves money on the table — often 5–15% of comp — because the candidate didn't realize the first company counter is typically only 40–60% movement toward the ask
warning_signs: You feel grateful rather than strategic after the first counter
You haven't yet attempted to shift levers like signing bonus or equity

failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates focus on what they want rather than what they'll do if they don't get it, treating the negotiation as a one-sided request rather than a bilateral decision
failure_patterns.consequence: Either accepts a package below their real floor, or overplays their hand with an arbitrary anchor and damages the offer
warning_signs: You haven't identified a specific walk-away number before the conversation
You're not sure whether you'd actually decline if the company doesn't move

failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates know competing offers are the strongest lever but don't have one, so they invent one to create urgency
failure_patterns.consequence: Recruiters verify offers; if caught, the offer is rescinded and professional trust is destroyed
warning_signs: You're tempted to reference a competing offer you don't actually have
You're unsure what details the company might ask to verify

failure_patterns.pattern: Continuing to push after all three levers have been addressed
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates don't track how many components they've already negotiated and keep pushing without recognizing that the negotiation space is exhausted
failure_patterns.consequence: Signals extraction-maximizing behavior, damages goodwill, and can cause a company to rescind or reduce advocacy for the candidate
warning_signs: You've already moved on base, equity, and signing bonus
The recruiter has volunteered that they've gone back to the hiring manager multiple times

failure_patterns.pattern: Misreading 'final offer' as always having room
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates learn that 'final offer' is often a negotiating tactic and apply that heuristic uniformly, even when the signal has shifted to genuinely final
failure_patterns.consequence: Pushes past the real ceiling, damages relationship, and occasionally triggers offer rescission
warning_signs: The recruiter's tone has shifted from sympathetic to matter-of-fact
A hard deadline has been attached to the final offer statement

diagnostic_questions.question: Do you have a specific number below which you will walk away from this offer?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the candidate has a real BATNA or is negotiating without an anchor
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Is that number based on a real alternative — current comp, competing offer — or an arbitrary preference?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Stop negotiating until you identify your walk-away number; without it you cannot negotiate effectively

diagnostic_questions.question: Do you have a competing offer, and would you genuinely consider taking it?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: The actual strength of your leverage; a competing offer you wouldn't take is weak leverage
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Share the number with the target company; you don't have to name the employer
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Assess whether you have time to generate one before your decision deadline

diagnostic_questions.question: How many rounds have you already completed, and which levers have you moved?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Where you are in the negotiation arc and how much room remains
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If you've addressed base, equity, and signing bonus across two or more rounds, you may be at or near the ceiling
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If you've only pushed on base, shift to other levers before concluding there's no room

diagnostic_questions.question: What is the recruiter's current tone — collaborative or administrative?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the company still sees room to move or has shifted into closure mode
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If collaborative, one more ask is likely acceptable; the recruiter may still be advocating for you
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If administrative or matter-of-fact, treat the current offer as the ceiling and decide whether to accept

diagnostic_questions.question: Where does this offer sit relative to the levels.fyi median for this role and level?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether market data supports continued negotiation or whether the offer is already at or above market
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If at or above median, your negotiating argument loses market-data support; focus on closing or non-cash levers
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If below median, market data is your strongest anchor for continued negotiation

diagnostic_questions.question: Is your offer deadline real or manufactured by the company?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether you have room to request an extension and use that time to generate competing offers
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If the deadline is company-imposed, request an extension framed as needing time for a thoughtful decision
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If the deadline is tied to a genuine competing offer expiration, use it as urgency with the target company

industry_realities.common_belief: Salary negotiation is a single conversation where you make one ask
industry_realities.actual_reality: Negotiation is a structured multi-round process with a predictable arc; the first counter is rarely the final one, and companies expect at least one or two rounds
industry_realities.implication: Candidates who stop after the first company counter routinely leave money on the table because they don't understand the expected arc

industry_realities.common_belief: 'Final offer' means the negotiation is over
industry_realities.actual_reality: The phrase 'final offer' is often a negotiating position, not a hard limit; the signal's meaning depends on delivery channel, tone, and whether a hard deadline is attached
industry_realities.implication: Assess context before taking 'final offer' at face value — an emailed 'final offer' from a sympathetic recruiter is different from the same phrase with a deadline on a phone call

industry_realities.common_belief: You need to name the competing company to make a competing offer credible
industry_realities.actual_reality: You only need to share the number; companies don't require — and recruiters don't always verify — the specific employer
industry_realities.implication: Share the dollar amount but withhold the company name to avoid unnecessary comparison and maintain negotiating simplicity

industry_realities.common_belief: Once you've signed an offer, negotiation is over
industry_realities.actual_reality: Post-acceptance negotiation is possible at 90-day reviews, when scope expands, or when market rates shift materially — but requires strong performance as the foundation
industry_realities.implication: Candidates who underestimate their value at signing can recover ground post-hire if they build a track record quickly and frame the ask around market data and delivered scope

industry_realities.common_belief: Companies have a fixed budget and all levers are equally constrained
industry_realities.actual_reality: Different comp components — base, signing bonus, equity — come from different budget pools with different levels of flexibility; base may be at ceiling while signing bonus has room
industry_realities.implication: When one lever is locked, shift to another rather than treating the whole package as immovable

industry_realities.common_belief: Generating urgency through a fake competing offer is a safe strategy
industry_realities.actual_reality: Recruiters verify competing offers, and fabricated offers are caught often enough that the risk is material; discovery leads to rescission and reputational damage
industry_realities.implication: Only use competing offer leverage when you have a real one; invest time in generating genuine competing offers rather than manufacturing fictitious ones

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Treats negotiation as a single event — makes one ask and either accepts or doesn't based on the response
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Understands the multi-round arc and paces asks across rounds, knowing when to push and when to close
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Juniors often stop at round one and leave 5–15% of comp on the table; seniors extract value across the full arc without damaging the relationship

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Enters negotiation hoping for a good outcome without pre-committing to a walk-away number
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Calculates a specific BATNA before the first conversation and treats it as a non-negotiable anchor throughout
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Without a BATNA, candidates either accept below their floor or overplay their hand; the BATNA prevents both mistakes

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Treats recruiter language as face value — takes 'final offer' literally, misses tone shifts
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Reads recruiter tone, delivery channel, and word choice as real-time signals of remaining room
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Misreading signals leads to either leaving money on the table or pushing past the real ceiling and damaging the offer

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Focuses exclusively on base salary and treats a ceiling there as the end of negotiation
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Tracks which levers have been used, shifts between base, equity, and signing bonus strategically, and only closes when all levers are exhausted
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Juniors miss compensation available in signing bonus or equity because they anchor entirely on base; seniors capture the full package

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Either doesn't have a competing offer or doesn't know how to use one; sometimes fabricates one
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Actively generates competing offers before deadlines to create real leverage, or uses the extension window strategically to do so
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Real competing offers are the strongest negotiation lever; seniors engineer the conditions to have one rather than hoping for it

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Optimizes purely for maximum extraction without considering how the negotiation process affects their reputation on day one
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Balances extraction with relationship preservation, knowing that goodwill with a hiring manager has long-term comp implications beyond the offer
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: A candidate perceived as difficult before starting may receive weaker advocacy in future reviews, costing them more than they gained in the negotiation
